question: Is it halal to eat shrimp, squid and other seafood, and why do some Muslims avoid it?
asked: I have been told that eating shrimp and squid is not allowed. How come some Muslims eat it and some Muslims don't?
answer:
So this is a very nice, succulent, juicy question. I'm not going to joke about seafood, because I see food and I like seafood, but I'm not going to joke about that, even though I just did. We're going to answer the question very simplistically.

Dear brother in Islam, the majority of madhhabs allow all types of animals that come from the ocean. This is something that the Maliki school, the Hanbali school and the Shafi'i school are very explicit on. These three madhhabs say that anything that lives in the ocean permanently (we're not talking about that which is half ocean, half water), anything that is predominantly in the water (by ocean we mean even rivers and lakes, any body of water), any animal whose primary existence is in the water, according to these three madhhabs, is allowed unconditionally, unless there is a poison in it that will harm you, unless there's something in it that's going to physically harm you. Otherwise, every animal from the water is allowed.

And the beauty of this is that by unanimous consensus, all the madhhabs say that you do not need to slaughter such an animal. You do not need to find it alive and then cut it like you have to do to hunted animals. No, you may find it dead. You may catch it and simply take it out of the water, and its death is its proper procedure for slaughtering. And so simply by taking the fish out of the water, whoever does it... And that's why even if you are strict on zabiha, you may eat seafood wherever you go, because it doesn't matter who caught it or how it was caught. With all seafood, the default is that it is halal.

Now, what is the evidence these scholars give on this issue? What is the evidence that all seafood is halal? They have a number of evidences. Primarily, there's a famous hadith and a famous verse of the Qur'an, Surah Al-Ma'idah verse 96. Allah says in the Qur'an that the catch of the ocean (notice the wording used, *sayd al-bahr*: you throw a net into the ocean and you take that net out; that is *sayd al-bahr*), so Allah is saying that the catch of the ocean, all of it, is permitted for you, and also even for the one in ihram.

Now, the one in ihram cannot hunt. You should know this: when you do Hajj or Umrah and you wear the ihram, you are not allowed to go and hunt animals. However, Allah allows the ocean traveler: if you're in ihram and you're on the ocean, so you're going from India to Hajj, let's say, and you are on the ocean, you're allowed to hunt fish, and you're allowed to eat anything that comes from the water. So Allah is saying that all of this is permitted for you. So the scholars say, when Allah said "the catch of the ocean," this means any animal that lives in the water is halal for us. And so this includes shrimps and squids and eels and octopus and all types of animals. It is halal, no exceptions.

Now, there's also a hadith of Abu Huraira reported in Abu Dawood, that somebody asked the Prophet ﷺ about doing wudu from ocean water. It's salty water, right? Can you do wudu from ocean water? And our Prophet ﷺ said that its water is halal to do wudu from, and its dead, anything that you find dead, is permitted for you to eat. You don't even have to catch it alive; if you find it dead in the ocean, it is halal for you to eat. *Huwa at-tahuru ma'uhu, al-hillu maytatuhu.* Notice he said "the dead of the ocean"; he did not say "the fish of the ocean." He said anything caught in the ocean.

And that is why we have explicit statements from many of the scholars of Islam. Even the great giants: Imam Malik, for example, said everything that lives in the ocean is edible. Everything, without exception, that lives in the ocean is edible, even if you find it floating dead on the top of the water. You may take it, no problem, because he said the Qur'an and Sunnah are very explicit on this point. **And this, inshallah ta'ala, is the correct position; it is the position I follow, and it is the one that the evidences support very clearly.** Therefore, according to that position, anything from the ocean, including seafood and shrimp and squid and octopus and lobsters, all of this would be completely permissible.

Now, what is the dissenting opinion? The dissenting opinion is the Hanafi school. And the Hanafi school is not explicit on this point; there are multiple positions even within the Hanafi school, and this is something that many modern Hanafis are not aware of, except the scholars who are familiar with this. Within the Hanafi school you have both of these opinions out there.

So for example, al-Kasani in his famous book *Bada'i' al-Sana'i'* (I spoke about this book in a previous lecture and mentioned the story of its writing, which is a very interesting story), al-Kasani says that the verse of the Qur'an, that the catch of the ocean is halal, and the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, that its dead is halal, only apply to samak, or fish. And he has his evidences that he brings; they have their way of basically restricting. So al-Kasani argues that we should not look at this verse and this hadith as unconditional. Rather, when our Prophet ﷺ says that its dead is halal, he means its fish are halal. And when Allah says that the catch of the ocean is halal, He means the fish is halal. And everything besides fish, according to al-Kasani, would not be allowed.

And that is why he and others would say that shrimp and prawns and other... By the way, shrimps and prawns, is there a difference between the two? It depends on which scientists you ask. Some say prawns are a type of shrimp, and some say prawns and shrimps are exactly the same. And technically speaking, prawns is a category. There are over 70 varieties of shrimp (yes, I've done my research), and one of them is basically a type, one category whose genus is called prawns. The point is that al-Kasani and others would say only fish is halal, and anything else that is not fish, including shrimps, including lobsters, would be...

Now, is it haram? No. No Hanafi scholar says it is haram. Rather, they say it is either makruh tahrimi or makruh tanzihi, because, again, the Hanafis have their categories. They would say it's makruh, either strongly or mildly. If it's strongly makruh, they would say that it's therefore a bit of a sin to eat. If it's slightly makruh, there is no sin in eating it, but it is better to avoid it. So that's the difference between makruh tahrimi and makruh tanzihi.

And among the evidences that the Hanafis use as well is the verse in the Qur'an that that which is filthy is forbidden. The *khabith* is forbidden. And they say that shrimp and lobsters are khabith, or filthy, and that we should not eat them. And the response is: who gets to define what is khabith, what is filthy and what is not filthy? The majority of other civilizations and scholars and madhhabs don't view these creatures to be filthy at all. So the notion goes, and you will find this in some fatwas, that "Oh, the shrimp, it is like the insects or the vermin of the ocean." And the response to this is: who said it's that type? Who is going to make this comparison? At the end of the day, when Allah has said the catch of the ocean is halal, and when the Prophet says that anything coming from the ocean, even its dead, is halal, then we should stick with that.

And by the way, what is also proven in this is that the Hanafi school says that fish is permitted, and by fish they don't mean the scientific term fish. Because by unanimous consensus, a whale is permissible to eat. We know this because the Prophet himself ate one. We know this because there's a hadith in Sahih Bukhari that the Sahaba were on the shores of the ocean and they found a dead whale, and they cut it up and ate it, and they brought some meat back to Medina, and the Prophet ﷺ himself ate from that. It was a whale. Now, technically, a whale is not a fish; a whale is a mammal. And yet it is allowed to eat, and the Hanafis also say this. So therefore, when they say fish is allowed, the response comes: who gets to define a fish?

And that is why even many modern Hanafis, and even some earlier ones as well, are saying, "Look, when the scholars say fish, what they mean is an animal of the ocean. It's not the biological definition of a fish." And the Darul Ifta of Egypt, which is the senior-most fatwa council of Egypt (and Egypt has a long tradition of Hanafi scholarship), gave a fatwa in which they said that shrimps should be considered a type of fish, samak, and they gave the fatwa that it should be allowed even according to the Hanafi madhhab, and there are Hanafis in that council as well.

However, you should know that the official fatwa of the Darul Uloom of Deoband, India, which is of course the main resource of our Indian, Pakistani and Bengali brethren of the Deobandi school, is that eating shrimp is makruh tanzihi: it is something that should be avoided, but it is not sinful. So that's the Darul Uloom Deoband fatwa. At the Darul Ifta of Egypt, the Hanafis there say that it's no problem; samak includes that as well.

And you will find even many modern Hanafi scholars (and I have many Hanafi friends, muftis of the Hanafi madhhab) who have told me that in their opinion the madhhab does not make it makruh tahrimi, and therefore they give the fatwa publicly that according to the Hanafi madhhab it should be allowed. But you should be aware that there are dissenting voices, and it is up to you what you want to do.

But if you ask me, **to me it is crystal clear that there is no evidence to forbid these items.** In fact, the Qur'an and Sunnah are very clear, and it is the vast majority position of the ummah. And also, even within the Hanafi school, we find many ulema that have explicitly allowed this.

And by the way, another point that demonstrates this is that some of our early Hanafi scholars explicitly mentioned the eel, and they said the eel is halal to eat, for example. And the eel is not a fish in the technical sense. You'll find this even in *al-Durr al-Mukhtar* and *I'la al-Sunan* of al-Tahanawi and others: they explicitly mention that the fish called al-marmahi, which is basically the eel, is allowed. Now why would the eel be allowed when it is not a fish in the technical sense, and the whale is allowed when it's not a fish in the technical sense, and then other animals that are also... So anyway, that's an internal discussion within the Hanafi madhhab. It's not my place to tell them what to say and what not to say.

I will simply state, since you're asking me the position that I would advise you: I would say it's not a problem if you eat this, and it is the majority position of our scholars. And if you choose to follow the position of Darul Uloom Deoband, that is also fine and permissible. And inshaAllah it is a matter in which both positions are... Allah knows best.
